message: foundry_verify scans the whole repo for every constraint on every task, and a constraint cannot declare "active from task X". On a brownfield repo whose pre-existing code already violates seeded constraints, the planner has to relocate legacy code outside the scanned paths, and has to defer regression-lock constraints to gate tasks that edit docs/foundry.json mid-flight. A per-constraint "since"/"activeFrom" task ID, or a baseline of pre-existing hits, would remove that workaround.

P0-16 asks to push the branch and check CI via gh. git push fails with "ERROR: This repository was archived so it is read-only" (same failure foundry_run_start reported as basePush at flight start). gh is installed and authenticated, but there is nothing to check CI against since the push never lands. This is an operator-level GitHub repo state issue, not something fixable from the worktree; logging it here so it's visible without blocking the task.

foundry_verify runs composer test (which does a fresh wp-env DB install) against the same shared test database as any other composer test invocation I have running. When I ran one in the background and called foundry_verify concurrently, both processes hit the same MySQL tables mid-install, producing spurious "table doesn't exist" and deadlock failures across unrelated tests (P1-08). No code defect; re-running foundry_verify alone was clean. Cost ~10 minutes diagnosing before realizing it was a self-inflicted concurrency issue, not a regression.

composer's default 300s process-timeout killed `composer test`'s host-side wrapper (npx wp-env run ...) mid-run, but the underlying `docker exec ... phpunit` process was NOT killed (npx/node detaches from the parent's process group), leaving it running inside the tests-cli container. Starting a second test invocation afterward ran concurrently against the same DB and produced real MySQL deadlocks and spurious failures, masking genuine results. Had to `docker exec ... ps aux | grep phpunit` and kill the orphaned PID inside the container before a clean rerun. Same root risk as the previously-logged overlapping-test-runs issue, but this time self-inflicted by composer's timeout rather than by me literally starting two runs.

Repeated, recurring flake across P2-04/05/06/07: WPPA_DAM=0 composer test intermittently fails a handful of tests with "Object of class WP_Error could not be converted to int" from tests/fixtures/class-v3-site.php:69 ($factory->attachment->create_upload_object() returning WP_Error), and once with a literal MySQL "Deadlock found when trying to get lock" on wp_postmeta during attachment metadata update. Not reproduced in isolated single-class runs; a clean re-run of the full suite always goes green. Costs ~7 minutes per retry. Root cause not investigated (outside this task's scope, and the fixture/DB config aren't touched by any of these tasks); worth a look if this project keeps hitting it.

foundry_mutate reports killed:true when the command failed only because an inner process timeout fired (composer's 300s process-timeout on `composer test`; an infinite-loop mutation in test:unit), so a timeout reads as a real kill. The timed-out run also left phpunit orphaned in the wp-env container, and the next mutation deadlocked on the DB. Suggest: set the verdict to 'inconclusive' when stderr shows a process timeout.

After a foundry_mutate run timed out, the orphaned phpunit kept running inside wp-env with the mutated Capabilities class loaded. It wrote the mutated role caps into the shared tests DB, and they survive the next phpunit install. A clean run then failed until the caps were removed by hand with wp-cli. foundry_mutate restores the file, but it cannot undo environment state that a mutated process writes after the tool gives up on it.

foundry_mutate reported killed:true for a Meta_Boxes mutation although `composer test` only timed out at its 1200000ms extraVerify limit (exitCode 0, timedOut true, no failures in 341/346 dots). A timeout is not a kill; the verdict should be 'inconclusive'. The full wp-env suite now takes ~1180s, so every integration mutation risks this false verdict.
